layout.title: Five-anomaly model evaluation
layout.notes: This deck replaces neither historical results nor their selection protocols. It consolidates the four-model comparison, expanded data, six actual visual fine-tunes, 330 strategy configurations, 50 video-pilot heads and 38 new ensemble/threshold policies, plus tracker and tiled-detector ablations. Candidate/prediction counts reuse sources and are not independent events. No deployment winner across all five objectives is established. No new latency benchmark was run. Stage-specific regressions and data limits remain visible.

layout.title: Five objectives require different evidence
layout.notes: The user accepted existing definitions and annotations. There is no newly invented universal loitering threshold. Public-sleep labels describe visible sleep/bedding/context, never housing status. AVSS specifies stationary for 30 seconds and an absent owner; historical provisional windows and MEVA abandonment actions do not uniformly implement this criterion. Grounding boxes and source annotations are separate from inferred ownership.

layout.title: Ranking, frame decisions and alerts are different
layout.notes: Pilot global rule:2s persistence,1s release,10s cooldown, reset for score gaps>1.1s. Thresholds maximize dev event recall within the stated normal false-alert budget. Strict matching counts only alert starts within positive intervals and separately reports repeated event alarms. Historical onset windows are provisional, so some unknown-time alarms may be useful early detections; do not portray those as proven normal false alarms. Overlapping windows do not create independent event observations. Confidence from a few cameras is limited.

layout.title: Ensembling improves HMDB; low-FPR CCTV remains hard
layout.notes: Each encoder compares 14 previous heads, four seed ensembles and one all-head ensemble: 19 policies. Equal sigmoid averages are not calibrated probabilities. layout.title: Explicit item state was more useful than a global score
layout.notes: Global alerts use two-second persistence, one-second release and ten-second cooldown. The one-false-alert/hour development target has only 28 seconds of dev normal footage and cannot certify that rate. Observed global normal rates are 21.7/hour and 130.3/hour. The separate AVSS source rule requires the same item stationary for 30 seconds and its associated owner absent. State-only results are independent of CLIP. The three videos appear to share one platform view; HARD remains a censored diagnostic.

layout.title: A good AP or zero observed alarms is not a guarantee
layout.notes: Entire ABODA classroom video7 and walkway video2 provide disjoint normal calibration and are excluded from both evaluation arms. Four events and 137 normal seconds remain. MobileCLIP detects 0/4 in both arms; SigLIP changes 0/4 to 1/4, with four normal false alerts reduced to one, still 26.3/hour. AVSS lacks disjoint normal calibration. Zero alarms over 165.74 normal seconds gives a one-sided 95% Poisson upper rate of 65.07/hour, assuming a homogeneous process. It is not a camera-transfer guarantee.

layout.title: More state machinery did not improve the AVSS result
layout.notes: The new rule uses three trailing centers and one second of sustained .015-frame displacement; pending motion blocks alerts. Item memory uses spatial one-to-one association and rearms on five seconds of owner return, three seconds of motion or 30 seconds absent. Synthetic tests cover simultaneous items and ID gaps without proving field benefits. AVSS stays 2/2 with zero false/repeated alerts; smoothing raises delay from 34.818 to 35.068 seconds. Memory raises HARD repeats from one to two. Historical intervals use different provisional definitions.

layout.title: Prioritize independently labelled target-camera evidence
